description:
Just a curious mind trying to make Earth sound interesting through NASA data. 🌍🎶
I'm a CSE student exploring tech, AI, and creative problem-solving. Still learning, occasionally debugging, and always ready to turn random ideas into something cool.
Our mission? Make something out of this world.  (And hopefully survive the debugging.)
summary:
Team NILANOVA developed EARTH JUKE, an interactive web-based project for NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026 – “The Earth Information Jukebox.” Our project combines interactive data visualizations and sonification to make Earth science easier to understand, explore, and experience.
The platform features four dashboards representing different Earth systems: the Cryosphere through Arctic Sea Ice, the Earth System through Global Temperature, the Biosphere through Forest Cover, and the Atmosphere through Carbon Dioxide levels.
The highlight of EARTH JUKE is sonification, which transforms scientific data into sound. Currently implemented in the Global Temperature dashboard, this feature represents temperature variations through changes in sound pitch, allowing users to hear environmental trends instead of simply observing graphs.
Our goal is to simplify complex scientific data, encourage interactive learning, and promote environmental awareness. In the future, we aim to extend sonification to all four dashboards.
Through EARTH JUKE, we aim to make Earth science not just informative but also an engaging sensory experience.
details:
Earth Juke is an interactive website designed to help people hear and see how our planet changes over time. It brings together the idea of exploring environmental signals such as temperature, Arctic sea ice, forest cover, and carbon dioxide through sound and visualization. Scientific datasets can be difficult to interpret without technical knowledge, so we wanted to turn those numbers into an experience that is easier to understand and explore.

For our current prototype, we implemented temperature sonification using 30 years of global temperature anomalies, from 1995 to 2024, collected from NASA’s GISS Surface Temperature Analysis dataset. These anomalies represent differences from a reference average rather than absolute temperatures. We used a small Python script to filter the required years from the larger dataset.

The main feature is sonification: converting data into sound. Each year’s temperature anomaly is mapped to a frequency, with higher anomalies producing higher pitches and lower anomalies producing lower pitches. Users can play, pause, reset, and adjust the playback speed and volume.

Alongside the sound, an animated graph highlights the corresponding year and temperature anomaly. Combining sound with a synchronized visual display lets users follow the same changes in two ways. This makes the experience more engaging than reading a table of numbers and helps listeners connect pitch changes with the actual temperature record.

We built the website using HTML, CSS, and JavaScript in Visual Studio Code. JavaScript’s Web Audio API generates the tones directly in the browser. We used Git and GitHub to collaborate and bring our contributions together.

Our intended impact is to support environmental awareness among students and the wider public. By making Earth science data easier to explore, we hope to encourage curiosity and conversations about our changing planet. The sound represents relative changes in the dataset; it is not a direct measure of danger or a warning system.

Our team considered reliable NASA data, clear sound mappings, synchronized visualization, and simple controls. Although the website introduces four environmental signals, temperature is the working feature in this prototype. We selected it as our starting point because it is an important indicator of climate change. Sonification of Arctic sea ice, forest cover, and carbon dioxide is planned for future development.

Data source: NASA GISS Surface Temperature Analysis (GISTEMP): https://data.giss.nasa.gov/gistemp/
